0fd97354-98a0-409c-aada-303dc78dbc87.title: WhatsApp Help Pages Leaked Hidden Instructions for a Meta Chatbot
0fd97354-98a0-409c-aada-303dc78dbc87.whatHappened: Around 80 pages on WhatsApp’s website exposed instructions that were designed for its chatbot, including “WHAT NOT TO SAY.”
evidence: A new analysis has found that around 80 help and FAQ pages across WhatsApp’s website exposed text instructions that were designed for a large language model, specifically one of Meta’s own.
Dozens of WhatsApp web pages designed to answer people’s questions about Meta’s encrypted messaging app inadvertently exposed the company’s own instructions to its chatbot.

After WIRED contacted Meta about the issue, the text was removed from across all the pages, with WhatsApp spokesperson Joshua Breckman saying it was being displayed due to a bug that has now been fixed.
The instructions, according to findings from privacy company Redact, appeared in the webpages’ code and contained written details that were not explicitly on the WhatsApp help pages.

“These are instructions to our chatbot, not directly to users, and are intended to ensure accurate and relevant responses for WhatsApp users who choose to message WhatsApp Support with AI,” Breckman says.

“Do not cite, quote, interpret, or reference WhatsApp Terms of Service, Privacy Policy, or any legal document,” the instructions said, adding not to make any statements about WhatsApp liability or non-liability.
WIRED viewed the exposed text, which can still be seen when viewing the underlying code of archived versions of the help pages.

Among the 100 blocks of hidden text, the directions appeared to provide guidance to steer an LLM from answering users questions in unhelpful ways and provide a glimpse at how instructions for chatbots are created.
Breckman, the WhatsApp spokesperson, says that the company provides users with transparent information about their data rights and how they can take actions.
“We want our product support chatbots to be focused on providing the best advice to users about WhatsApp—not to offer legal advice,” Breckman says.

He says the company regularly scans the sites and privacy policies of big tech firms, and that many of the WhatsApp instructions the team found were straightforward and point people towards other official support channels.
Still, it does not appear the instructions were meant for public exposure.

ec4444ea-5e26-42c0-8713-83ed434fd97a.title: FairStress: A deeper evaluation of fairness in LLM decision-making
evidence: On FairStress-Core, frontier models including Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.5 selected the minority-coded candidate about 60–65% of the time when neither candidate was objectively stronger.
Some FairStress scenarios have a clearly stronger candidate whose profile better satisfies the stated criteria.
FairStress shows why a model’s demographic fairness can’t be judged solely by whether it reaches the same final choice across otherwise equivalent scenarios.
Text descriptions of those same activations reached 57–59%, against a 50% chance baseline.
Standard demographic fairness benchmarks often test whether a model selects the same candidate in otherwise identical scenarios after the candidates’ demographic identities are swapped.
FairStress is designed to measure these hidden asymmetries.
FairStress does not attempt to capture every conception of fairness.

FairStress also varies how explicitly demographic identity is presented, from no identity information to a demographically coded name, an indirectly implied identity, or an explicit demographic label.
Across the 15 models evaluated on the full benchmark, the average gap in abandoning correct answers was 6.9 percentage points with implied identity and 9.3 points with explicit labels.
FairStress can also be used to evaluate whether debiasing techniques actually produce more robust, fairer model behavior.

Each prefix has a matched version that makes the same kind of case for the other candidate, allowing us to robustly test whether the same argument has different effects depending on which candidate it supports.
Combining these variations in demographic identity and prefix expands FairStress’ 300 scenarios into more than 13 million test cases.
